questions.stem: A 27 year old teacher has had 5 months of episodic wheeze, chest tightness and a dry cough. Symptoms wake her at about 4 am and are worse when she visits her sister, who has a cat. She has hay fever. Between episodes her chest is clear. Her FEV1/FVC is 0.66 and FEV1 rises by 17% after salbutamol.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Variable, nocturnal, triggered wheeze with reversibility = asthma. Why not Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease? She is young, with variable symptoms and marked reversibility.

steps.x: Episodic, variable, worse early morning, cat trigger, atopy, reversibility over 12%.

elim: She is young, with variable symptoms and marked reversibility.
A short post-viral illness, not 5 months of episodic symptoms.
Acute, with rash, angioedema and hypotension, not months of episodes.

steps.x: **C. Asthma.** Variable, nocturnal, triggered wheeze with reversibility = asthma.

questions.stem: A 9 year old boy has a recurrent cough at night and wheeze when he plays football. He had eczema as a baby and his mother has hay fever. His father smokes indoors. Examination between episodes is normal. His GP is considering a chronic airway disease.
questions.q: Which feature in his history most increases the likelihood of asthma?
questions.e: Atopy, family history, allergens and smoking raise asthma risk; it often begins in childhood. Why not Normal examination between episodes? Expected in asthma but does not raise the likelihood.

steps.x: Atopy (eczema) plus family history and smoke.

elim: Viral-induced cough alone is less specific.
Expected in asthma but does not raise the likelihood.
Exercise wheeze occurs in asthma but atopy is the stronger risk factor.

steps.x: **C. Personal history of eczema.** Atopy, family history, allergens and smoking raise asthma risk; it often begins in childhood.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man works in a factory making polyurethane foam. He had no chest problems until a year ago. He now has wheeze and chest tightness that are worse at the end of each working week and better after 2 weeks on holiday. He has never smoked.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Adult-onset asthma that improves away from work = occupational asthma, most often isocyanates. Why not Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease? He has never smoked and symptoms improve away from work.

steps.x: Adult onset, foam (isocyanates), better on holiday.

elim: He has never smoked and symptoms improve away from work.
Causes fever, crackles and restrictive spirometry.
Typical of healthcare workers, with urticaria.
A fibrotic disease of miners and stonemasons, not work-related variable wheeze.

steps.x: **D. Occupational asthma.** Adult-onset asthma that improves away from work = occupational asthma, most often isocyanates.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman with asthma uses low-dose MART. Over 2 months she has used her inhaler for symptoms on 4 days a week, woken with wheeze twice a week and stopped going to the gym. Her inhaler technique and adherence are good.
questions.q: Which feature best shows her asthma is poorly controlled?
o: Symptoms on 3 or more days a week
questions.e: Poor control: daytime symptoms 3 or more times a week, night waking, reduced exercise tolerance, recent attack. Why not Good inhaler technique? Good technique is required before stepping up but does not show poor control.

clues: woken with wheeze twice a week
steps.x: Daytime symptoms 4 days a week, night waking, reduced exercise.

elim: Good technique is required before stepping up but does not show poor control.
Old normal lung function says nothing about current control.
Being on a regimen is not a sign of control.
Not what she has, and would not mark poor control on its own.

steps.x: **C. Symptoms on 3 or more days a week.** Poor control: daytime symptoms 3 or more times a week, night waking, reduced exercise tolerance, recent attack.

questions.stem: A 21 year old student with asthma attends for her annual review. She has had no symptoms in the day or night, has not used her reliever, has had no attacks and plays netball. Spirometry is normal and she has no side effects.
questions.q: Which best describes her asthma?
questions.e: Complete control = no symptoms, no rescue use, no exacerbations, no limitation, normal lung function, minimal side effects. Why not Near-fatal asthma? Describes a severe attack with raised CO2.

steps.x: No symptoms, no reliever, no attacks, no limitation, normal lung function.

elim: Describes a severe attack with raised CO2.
She has no symptoms, reliever use or limitation.
Uncontrolled despite maximal therapy; she is symptom-free.

steps.x: **E. Well controlled.** Complete control = no symptoms, no rescue use, no exacerbations, no limitation, normal lung function, minimal side effects.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman with adult-onset asthma has had three attacks in a year. Each began within an hour of taking ibuprofen for back pain. She has a constantly blocked nose and has lost her sense of smell. Nasal endoscopy shows pale grape-like masses.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Samter's triad (AERD) = asthma, nasal polyps, aspirin/NSAID sensitivity. Why not Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis? Causes eosinophilia and bronchiectasis, not NSAID-triggered attacks with polyps.

clues: within an hour of taking ibuprofen
steps.x: Asthma + nasal polyps + NSAID-triggered attacks.

elim: Causes eosinophilia and bronchiectasis, not NSAID-triggered attacks with polyps.
Asthma with vasculitis and neuropathy, not NSAID sensitivity.
Polyps occur but in the young, with bronchiectasis and malabsorption.
Causes nasal crusting and bleeding, with renal disease.

steps.x: **E. Samter's triad.** Samter's triad (AERD) = asthma, nasal polyps, aspirin/NSAID sensitivity.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man dies from a sudden severe asthma attack. At post-mortem the airways are filled with thick mucus. Microscopy of the sputum taken shortly before death shows coiled, spiral-shaped mucus casts of the small airways.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding being described?
questions.e: Curschmann spirals are mucus plugs shed from small airways in asthma. Why not Asbestos bodies? Found in asbestos exposure.

steps.x: Coiled spiral mucus casts in asthma.

elim: Eosinophil-derived crystals, not spiral mucus casts.

steps.x: **C. Curschmann spirals.** Curschmann spirals are mucus plugs shed from small airways in asthma.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has had asthma since childhood. Over a year he has had worsening wheeze and cough with brown sputum plugs. His blood eosinophil count is 1.6 ×10⁹/L and total IgE is very high. CT chest shows central bronchiectasis.
questions.q: Which complication of asthma is most likely?
questions.e: ABPA complicates asthma or bronchiectasis with wheeze and eosinophilia. Why not Acute eosinophilic pneumonia? Acute illness with respiratory failure, not a year of plugs and bronchiectasis.

steps.x: Long asthma history, brown plugs, eosinophilia, high IgE, central bronchiectasis.

elim: Acute illness with respiratory failure, not a year of plugs and bronchiectasis.
A fungal ball in an old cavity, without high IgE and eosinophilia.
Causes weight loss, sweats and upper lobe cavities.

steps.x: **B. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.** ABPA complicates asthma or bronchiectasis with wheeze and eosinophilia.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man with asthma has had increasing wheeze for 2 days. He can talk in full sentences. His pulse rate is 98 bpm, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. His PEF is 330 L/min; his best is 520 L/min (63%).

visual.title: PEF, % of best
visual.label: Today 63%
visual.caption: BTS/SIGN bands: moderate 50-75%, acute severe 33-50%, life-threatening below 33%.

questions.q: Which is the most likely severity of this exacerbation?
questions.e: Moderate = PEF 50-75% with no features of acute severe asthma. Why not Acute severe asthma? Needs PEF 33-50%, RR 25 or more, HR 110 or more, or incomplete sentences.

steps.x: PEF 63% of best, full sentences, normal RR and HR.

elim: Needs PEF 33-50%, RR 25 or more, HR 110 or more, or incomplete sentences.
Needs PEF below 33% or sats below 92%.
Needs a raised CO2 or ventilation.

steps.x: **C. Moderate exacerbation.** Moderate = PEF 50-75% with no features of acute severe asthma.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman with asthma has 1 day of worsening breathlessness. She stops after every few words. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Her PEF is 42% of her best. She is alert.

visual.title: PEF, % of best
visual.label: Today 42%
visual.caption: BTS/SIGN bands: moderate 50-75%, acute severe 33-50%, life-threatening below 33%.

questions.q: Which is the most likely severity of this attack?
questions.e: Acute severe = PEF 33-50%, RR 25 or more, HR 110 or more, cannot complete sentences. Why not Life-threatening asthma? Sats are above 92%, PEF above 33% and she is alert.

steps.x: PEF 42%, RR 28, HR 118, cannot complete sentences, sats 95%.

elim: Sats are above 92%, PEF above 33% and she is alert.
PEF below 50%, tachycardia and tachypnoea exceed moderate.
A trigger pattern, not a severity grade.

steps.x: **A. Acute severe asthma.** Acute severe = PEF 33-50%, RR 25 or more, HR 110 or more, cannot complete sentences.

questions.stem: A 17 year old girl with asthma is brought to the emergency department. She is confused and has blue lips. Her pulse rate is 125 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. Her chest is almost silent.
questions.q: Which is the most likely severity of this attack?
questions.e: A CHEST 92: Altered consciousness, Cyanosis, Hypotension, Exhaustion, Silent chest, Tachy/brady, sats below 92%. Why not Acute severe asthma? Sats below 92%, confusion, cyanosis, hypotension and silent chest make this life-threatening.

steps.x: Confusion, cyanosis, hypotension, sats 89%, silent chest.

elim: Sats below 92%, confusion, cyanosis, hypotension and silent chest make this life-threatening.
No allergen, rash or angioedema; she has known asthma.
Would cause unilateral absent breath sounds and tracheal shift.

steps.x: **C. Life-threatening asthma.** A CHEST 92: Altered consciousness, Cyanosis, Hypotension, Exhaustion, Silent chest, Tachy/brady, sats below 92%.

questions.stem: A 23 year old man has acute severe asthma. His oxygen saturation is 90% breathing air and his respiratory rate is 32 breaths per minute. Arterial blood gas taken on air shows: pH 7.38, PaO2 7.9 kPa, PaCO2 5.4 kPa.
questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of the PaCO2?
o: Acute severe asthma with appropriate hyperventilation
Life-threatening asthma with a worrying normal PaCO2
questions.e: ABG if sats below 92%; a normal PaCO2 (4.6-6.0) in a severe attack is life-threatening. Why not Acute severe asthma with appropriate hyperventilation? In a severe attack the PaCO2 should be low; normal is ominous.

steps.x: Sats 90%, PaO2 low, PaCO2 'normal' despite RR 32.

elim: In a severe attack the PaCO2 should be low; normal is ominous.
No raised bicarbonate or chronic CO2 retention.

steps.x: **C. Life-threatening asthma with a worrying normal PaCO2.** ABG if sats below 92%; a normal PaCO2 (4.6-6.0) in a severe attack is life-threatening.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman with asthma is in resuscitation. Despite nebulisers, steroids and IV magnesium she is drowsy with a respiratory rate of 10 breaths per minute. ABG shows pH 7.18 and PaCO2 8.9 kPa.
questions.q: Which is the most likely severity of this attack?
questions.e: Near-fatal = raised CO2 and/or need for ventilation with raised inflation pressures. Why not Acute severe asthma? A raised CO2 and drowsiness go beyond acute severe.

clues: drowsy with a respiratory rate of 10
steps.x: Raised PaCO2 with acidosis and falling respiratory rate.

elim: A raised CO2 and drowsiness go beyond acute severe.
The pH is very low; there is no compensation.
No opioid history; she is tiring from asthma.

steps.x: **D. Near-fatal asthma.** Near-fatal = raised CO2 and/or need for ventilation with raised inflation pressures.

questions.stem: A 14 year old girl has a cough that is worse at night and in the early morning. She wheezes when near cigarette smoke. On examination during a symptomatic visit there is widespread polyphonic wheeze with a prolonged expiratory phase. Her PEF varies between 250 and 380 L/min.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Variable airflow obstruction with nocturnal and triggered symptoms = asthma. Why not Aspiration of a foreign body? Sudden onset, unilateral monophonic wheeze.

clues: worse at night and in the early morning
steps.x: Nocturnal cough, smoke trigger, prolonged expiration, variable PEF.

elim: A short post-viral cough, not recurrent variable symptoms.
Nasal symptoms, not wheeze and variable PEF.

steps.x: **E. Asthma.** Variable airflow obstruction with nocturnal and triggered symptoms = asthma.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman with asthma develops wheeze, sneezing and itchy eyes within 15 minutes of entering a house with a dog. Her blood total IgE is raised and skin prick testing to dog dander is positive.
questions.q: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction best explains her attack?
questions.e: Asthma is a Type I (IgE, immediate) hypersensitivity causing reversible obstruction. Why not Type II hypersensitivity? Antibody against cell surface antigens, e.g. haemolysis.

steps.x: Immediate reaction within minutes, raised IgE, positive skin prick.

elim: Antibody against cell surface antigens, e.g. haemolysis.
Immune complex deposition, e.g. hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

steps.x: **A. Type I hypersensitivity.** Asthma is a Type I (IgE, immediate) hypersensitivity causing reversible obstruction.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man with asthma uses low-dose MART. In the last 2 years he was admitted once with an attack. He now notices his inhaler helps less than before and he gets breathless walking his dog. He has no night symptoms.
questions.q: Which feature indicates poor asthma control?
questions.e: Poor control: reduced bronchodilator effect, reduced exercise tolerance, an attack within 2 years. Why not Absence of night symptoms? A sign of better, not worse, control.

steps.x: Inhaler helps less, reduced exercise tolerance, attack within 2 years.

elim: A sign of better, not worse, control.
A possible trigger, not a control marker.
Treatment choice, not a sign of control.

steps.x: **D. Reduced effect of his bronchodilator.** Poor control: reduced bronchodilator effect, reduced exercise tolerance, an attack within 2 years.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman with long-standing asthma has had poorly controlled symptoms for 6 months with fleeting shadows on chest X-ray. Her blood eosinophils are 2.1 ×10⁹/L. Aspergillus-specific IgE is raised and skin testing to Aspergillus fumigatus is positive.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: ABPA: asthma + eosinophilia + Aspergillus sensitisation. Why not Acute eosinophilic pneumonia? Acute illness with respiratory failure, no Aspergillus sensitisation.

steps.x: Asthma, fleeting shadows, marked eosinophilia, Aspergillus sensitisation.

elim: Acute illness with respiratory failure, no Aspergillus sensitisation.
A fungal ball in a pre-existing cavity.
Antigen exposure such as birds; restrictive pattern.

steps.x: **B. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.** ABPA: asthma + eosinophilia + Aspergillus sensitisation.

questions.stem: A 32 year old man has 4 months of episodic wheeze and night cough. His blood eosinophil count is normal and FeNO is not available at his practice. Spirometry shows FEV1 2.9 L and FVC 4.4 L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm asthma?
questions.e: Spirometry with reversibility: an FEV1 rise of 12% or more after salbutamol supports asthma. Why not Chest X-ray? Usually normal in asthma and does not confirm it.

steps.x: Obstructive spirometry (ratio 0.66), suspected asthma.

elim: Usually normal in asthma and does not confirm it.
Shows atopy, not variable airflow obstruction.

steps.x: **D. Spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility.** Spirometry with reversibility: an FEV1 rise of 12% or more after salbutamol supports asthma.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has had 3 months of episodic wheeze, chest tightness and night cough, worse with cold air. She has hay fever. Her chest is clear today. She has spirometry before salbutamol in the GP practice. Her predicted FVC is 3.8 L and she has suspected asthma.
questions.q: Which result is most consistent with asthma?
questions.e: Obstructive: low FEV1, reduced FEV1/FVC (below 0.7), preserved FVC. Why not FEV1 2.6 L, FVC 2.9 L, FEV1/FVC 0.90? A restrictive pattern with low FVC.

steps.x: Asthma gives an obstructive pattern.

elim: A restrictive pattern with low FVC.
Restrictive: both reduced with a normal ratio.

steps.x: **C. FEV1 2.2 L, FVC 3.7 L, FEV1/FVC 0.59.** Obstructive: low FEV1, reduced FEV1/FVC (below 0.7), preserved FVC.

questions.stem: A 10 year old boy has nocturnal cough and wheeze. He has eczema and his symptoms are worse in spring. His chest is clear today and he is growing normally. His FeNO is 22 ppb. His GP wants a further test to confirm or rule out asthma.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Children: if FeNO is not raised, do BDR; FEV1 rise of 12% or more (or 10% predicted) is diagnostic. Why not Bronchial challenge test first? Used if earlier tests are unclear.

steps.x: Child 5-16 with FeNO below 35 ppb.

elim: Used if earlier tests are unclear.

steps.x: **B. Bronchodilator reversibility on spirometry.** Children: if FeNO is not raised, do BDR; FEV1 rise of 12% or more (or 10% predicted) is diagnostic.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has variable wheeze and nocturnal cough for 3 months. She has eczema and her symptoms are worse in winter. Her chest is clear between episodes and she has never smoked. Her GP practice does not have FeNO. A full blood count is taken.
questions.q: Which result would best support a diagnosis of asthma?
questions.e: In primary care a blood eosinophil count above the upper limit (0.4 ×10⁹/L) supports asthma. Why not Basophils 0.05 ×10⁹/L? Normal and not used for diagnosis.

steps.x: FeNO not available; blood count taken.

elim: Normal and not used for diagnosis.
Neutrophilia suggests infection, not eosinophilic asthma.

steps.x: **B. Eosinophils 0.6 ×10⁹/L.** In primary care a blood eosinophil count above the upper limit (0.4 ×10⁹/L) supports asthma.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has 6 months of wheeze and cough. Symptoms wake him at night and are worse near his partner's cat. He has never smoked and his chest is clear today. His fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) is 68 ppb. He is on no inhalers.
questions.q: What does this result most likely indicate?
questions.e: FeNO above 50 ppb supports asthma and reflects eosinophilic (Th2) inflammation. Why not Bacterial bronchitis? Neutrophilic, does not raise FeNO.

steps.x: FeNO above 50 ppb.

elim: FeNO does not measure fixed obstruction.

steps.x: **B. Eosinophilic airway inflammation.** FeNO above 50 ppb supports asthma and reflects eosinophilic (Th2) inflammation.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has 3 months of intermittent cough and wheeze, worse in the mornings and after exercise. He has hay fever. His chest is clear in clinic. Spirometry cannot be arranged for some weeks. He records twice-daily peak flow for 2 weeks.
questions.q: Which result would best support a diagnosis of asthma?
questions.e: PEF variability over 20% supports asthma when spirometry is unavailable. Why not Constant peak flow of 520 L/min? No variability.

steps.x: Spirometry unavailable, 2 weeks of twice-daily PEF.
**D. Peak flow variability above 20%.** PEF variability over 20% supports asthma when spirometry is unavailable.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has symptoms suggesting asthma. Her FeNO is 30 ppb, eosinophils are normal, reversibility testing shows an FEV1 rise of 7% and a peak flow diary shows 14% variability. She has never smoked and her chest is clear. The diagnosis remains unclear.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: If the diagnosis is unclear after FeNO, eosinophils, BDR and PEF, do a bronchial challenge test. Why not CT pulmonary angiogram? Looks for pulmonary embolism.

steps.x: All earlier tests are inconclusive.

elim: For interstitial lung disease or bronchiectasis.
Unlikely to change and delays diagnosis.

steps.x: **B. Direct bronchial challenge test.** If the diagnosis is unclear after FeNO, eosinophils, BDR and PEF, do a bronchial challenge test.

questions.stem: A 39 year old hairdresser has had wheeze and cough for a year, starting after she began using bleaching products. Symptoms ease at weekends and on holiday. She had no chest problems before and has never smoked. Her GP suspects occupational asthma.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Serial peak flow at work and away from work
questions.e: Occupational asthma: serial PEF at work and home to show the work pattern. Why not Chest X-ray? Normal in asthma.

steps.x: Adult-onset wheeze that improves away from work.

elim: Does not show the work link.
One reading cannot show the link with work.

steps.x: **D. Serial peak flow at work and away from work.** Occupational asthma: serial PEF at work and home to show the work pattern.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man has acute severe asthma. He has received oxygen and back-to-back nebulised salbutamol. His pulse rate is 124 bpm and respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute. His oxygen saturation is 91% on 15 L/min oxygen and he is tiring.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: ABG is needed if sats are below 92% to look for a normal or raised PaCO2. Why not Chest X-ray before treatment? Should not delay assessment of gas exchange.

steps.x: Sats below 92% in an acute attack.

elim: Should not delay assessment of gas exchange.
Not possible in an acute attack.

steps.x: **A. Arterial blood gas.** ABG is needed if sats are below 92% to look for a normal or raised PaCO2.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman is newly diagnosed with asthma after a FeNO of 55 ppb. She has wheeze and chest tightness 2 days a week and no night waking. She has never had an attack needing hospital care. Her chest is clear today. She asks about the inhaler she will start.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: First-line in adults: as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol, and rinse the mouth after use. Why not Oral montelukast alone? An add-on, not first-line.

steps.x: New adult asthma, not severe.

elim: LABA without ICS is unsafe in asthma.
A LAMA used later as an add-on.
SABA without ICS does not treat inflammation.

steps.x: **A. As-needed low-dose budesonide/formoterol.** First-line in adults: as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol, and rinse the mouth after use.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man is newly diagnosed with asthma. He has symptoms most days, wakes most nights and was seen in the emergency department last week with a severe attack needing oral steroids. His FEV1 rose by 22% after salbutamol. He has never used an inhaler before.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: If severe at diagnosis, start at the second step: low-dose MART. Why not As-needed salbutamol only? No anti-inflammatory therapy.

steps.x: Severe exacerbation at diagnosis.

elim: Too little given his severe presentation.
Too high a step to start.

steps.x: **C. Low-dose MART.** If severe at diagnosis, start at the second step: low-dose MART.

questions.stem: An 8 year old girl with asthma has ongoing symptoms despite SABA with a paediatric low-dose ICS. She uses her reliever 4 times a week and her technique with a spacer is good. Her doctor considers moving her to a MART regimen.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate step before starting MART?
o: Refer to a specialist straight away
Teach and confirm she can manage MART
questions.e: In children, check that the child can manage MART before starting it. Why not Check her urea and electrolytes? Not needed for MART.

clues: considers moving her to a MART regimen
steps.x: Child moving onto MART.

elim: She is not yet at that step.

steps.x: **E. Teach and confirm she can manage MART.** In children, check that the child can manage MART before starting it.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man with asthma uses low-dose budesonide/formoterol as maintenance and reliever. Despite good technique and adherence he still has daytime symptoms 4 times a week and wakes once a week. His FeNO is 30 ppb. He works as a postman.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Low-dose MART, then moderate-dose MART. Why not Add oral theophylline? Not part of the current pathway.

clues: low-dose budesonide/formoterol as maintenance and reliever
steps.x: Uncontrolled on low-dose MART.

elim: Not part of the current pathway.
Comes after moderate MART and add-ons.

steps.x: **C. Increase to moderate-dose MART.** Low-dose MART, then moderate-dose MART.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman with asthma is on moderate-dose MART with good adherence and technique and still has symptoms. She wakes with wheeze twice a week. Her FeNO is 18 ppb and blood eosinophils are 0.2 ×10⁹/L.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Trial of montelukast added to moderate-dose MART
questions.e: Fourth step: if FeNO and eosinophils are not raised, trial an LTRA or LAMA with moderate MART. Why not Refer for biologic therapy? Biologics are for raised FeNO or eosinophils via a specialist.

steps.x: Uncontrolled on moderate MART, FeNO and eosinophils not raised.

elim: Biologics are for raised FeNO or eosinophils via a specialist.

steps.x: **E. Trial of montelukast added to moderate-dose MART.** Fourth step: if FeNO and eosinophils are not raised, trial an LTRA or LAMA with moderate MART.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with asthma is on moderate-dose MART and still has frequent symptoms despite good adherence. He has had two courses of oral steroids this year. His FeNO is 74 ppb and blood eosinophils are 0.9 ×10⁹/L.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Add montelukast and review in a year
questions.e: Raised FeNO or eosinophils on moderate MART = refer to specialist (e.g. for biologics). Why not Add montelukast and review in a year? Raised markers mean specialist referral.

steps.x: Uncontrolled on moderate MART with raised FeNO and eosinophils.
**D. Refer to an asthma specialist.** Raised FeNO or eosinophils on moderate MART = refer to specialist (e.g. for biologics).

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with asthma on moderate-dose MART has had no symptoms for 5 months. She uses her reliever once a month, has had no attacks for over a year, sleeps well and her PEF is near her best.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Stop the ICS and continue LABA
questions.e: Step down after at least 3 months of good control: reduce ICS by 25-50% and monitor. Why not Continue unchanged indefinitely? Step down once control is sustained.

steps.x: Over 3 months of good control on moderate MART.

elim: Step down once control is sustained.
Stopping ICS risks loss of control.

steps.x: **B. Reduce the ICS dose by 25-50%.** Step down after at least 3 months of good control: reduce ICS by 25-50% and monitor.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man has acute severe asthma. His oxygen saturation is 92% breathing air, pulse rate 116 bpm and respiratory rate 27 breaths per minute. He cannot complete sentences and his PEF is 40% of best. He can swallow and is not vomiting.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Oxygen, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, oral prednisolone
questions.e: Target sats 94-98%; nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium in oxygen with prednisolone 40-50 mg. Why not IV aminophylline first? Second-line after magnesium in refractory attacks.

steps.x: Sats 92%, acute severe, can take oral medication.

elim: Second-line after magnesium in refractory attacks.
Steroids alone are not enough; oral prednisolone is preferred.

steps.x: **E. Oxygen, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, oral prednisolone.** Target sats 94-98%; nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium in oxygen with prednisolone 40-50 mg.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman who is 30 weeks pregnant has acute severe asthma. After oxygen, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, and oral prednisolone, her PEF has risen from 45% to 70% of best and she feels much better.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Discharge with a salbutamol inhaler only
questions.e: Pregnant women with a severe attack are admitted even if they improve; discharge needs PEF over 75%. Why not Discharge with oral prednisolone? Pregnant women with severe attacks are admitted even if better.

steps.x: Pregnant, severe attack, now improved.

elim: Pregnant women with severe attacks are admitted even if better.
Not long enough, and pregnancy needs admission.

steps.x: **A. Admit to hospital.** Pregnant women with a severe attack are admitted even if they improve; discharge needs PEF over 75%.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has acute severe asthma. After 1 hour of oxygen, back-to-back nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium and oral prednisolone 40 mg, his PEF is still 38% of best and he cannot complete sentences.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Refractory attack: IV magnesium first, then aminophylline, then IV salbutamol, then intubation. Why not IV aminophylline? Given after magnesium.

steps.x: Not responding to first-line therapy.

elim: A last resort in life-threatening asthma.

steps.x: **B. IV magnesium sulphate.** Refractory attack: IV magnesium first, then aminophylline, then IV salbutamol, then intubation.

o: Stimulation of beta-2 receptors raising cAMP

questions.stem: A 21 year old woman with acute severe asthma had a PaCO2 of 3.6 kPa on arrival. Her respiratory rate was 34 breaths per minute. Two hours later, despite treatment, she is quieter, her respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute and her PaCO2 is 5.6 kPa.

questions.e: A normalising or rising PaCO2 means she is tiring and can no longer maintain ventilation. Why not Improving bronchospasm? She is quieter and worsening, not better.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman and a 65 year old ex-smoker both have FEV1/FVC 0.62. After salbutamol her FEV1 rises by 18%, his by 4%. Both have breathlessness on exertion. A student asks what this difference shows.

o: Reversible bronchoconstriction relieved by a beta-2 agonist
questions.e: Reversible obstruction (12% or more) separates asthma from COPD. Why not Fixed alveolar destruction? Explains his minimal reversibility (COPD).
